w-problem-of-time: In theoretical physics, the problem of time is a conceptual conflict between quantum mechanics and general relativity. Quantum mechanics regards the flow of time as universal and absolute, whereas general relativity regards the flow of time as malleable and relative. This problem raises the question of what time really is in a physical sense and whether it is truly a real, distinct phenomenon. It also involves the related question of why time seems to flow in a single direction, despite the fact that no known physical laws at the microscopic level seem to require a single direction.
## Time in quantum mechanics

In classical mechanics, a special status is assigned to time in the sense that it is treated as a classical background parameter, external to the system itself. This special role is seen in the standard Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics: all measurements of observables are made at certain instants of time and probabilities are only assigned to such measurements. Furthermore, the Hilbert space used in quantum theory relies on a complete set of observables which commute at a specific time.
## Time in general relativity

In general relativity time is no longer a unique background parameter, but a general coordinate. The field equations of general relativity are not parameterized by time but formulated in terms of spacetime. Many of the issues related to the problem of time exist within general relativity. At the cosmic scale, general relativity shows a closed universe with no external time. These two very different roles of time are incompatible.
## Impact on quantum gravity

Quantum gravity describes theories that attempt to reconcile or unify quantum mechanics and general relativity, the current theory of gravity. The problem of time is central to these theoretical attempts. It remains unclear how time is related to quantum probability, whether time is fundamental or a consequence of processes, and whether time is approximate, among other issues. Different theories try different answers to the questions but no clear solution has emerged.

## Proposed solutions to the problem of time

Work started by Don Page and William Wootters suggests that the universe appears to evolve for observers on the inside because of energy entanglement between an evolving system and a clock system, both within the universe. In this way the overall system can remain timeless while parts experience time via entanglement. The issue remains an open question closely related to attempted theories of quantum gravity.
In other words, time is an entanglement phenomenon, which places all equal clock readings (of correctly prepared clocks – or any objects usable as clocks) into the same history.

In 2013, at the Istituto Nazionale di Ricerca Metrologica (INRIM) in Turin, Italy, Ekaterina Moreva, together with Giorgio Brida, Marco Gramegna, Vittorio Giovannetti, Lorenzo Maccone, and Marco Genovese performed the first experimental test of Page and Wootters' ideas. They confirmed for photons that time is an emergent phenomenon for internal observers of a quantum system but is absent for external observers, which is consistent with the predictions of the Wheeler–DeWitt equation.

Consistent discretizations approach developed by Jorge Pullin and Rodolfo Gambini have no constraints. These are lattice approximation techniques for quantum gravity. In the canonical approach, if one discretizes the constraints and equations of motion, the resulting discrete equations are inconsistent: they cannot be solved simultaneously. To address this problem, one uses a technique based on discretizing the action of the theory and working with the discrete equations of motion. These are automatically guaranteed to be consistent. Most of the hard conceptual questions of quantum gravity are related to the presence of constraints in the theory. Consistent discretized theories are free of these conceptual problems and can be straightforwardly quantized, providing a solution to the problem of time. It is a bit more subtle than this. Although without constraints and having "general evolution", the latter is only in terms of a discrete parameter that isn't physically accessible. The way out is addressed in a way similar to the Page–Wootters approach. The idea is to pick one of the physical variables to be a clock and ask relational questions. These ideas, where the clock is also quantum mechanical, have actually led to a new interpretation of quantum mechanics — the Montevideo interpretation of quantum mechanics. This new interpretation solves the problems of the use of environmental decoherence as a solution to the problem of measurement in quantum mechanics by invoking fundamental limitations, due to the quantum mechanical nature of clocks, in the process of measurement. These limitations are very natural in the context of generally covariant theories as quantum gravity where the clock must be taken as one of the degrees of freedom of the system itself. They have also put forward this fundamental decoherence as a way to resolve the black hole information paradox. In certain circumstances, a matter field is used to de-parametrize the theory and introduce a physical Hamiltonian. This generates physical time evolution, not a constraint.

Reduced phase-space quantization constraints are solved first and then quantized. This approach was considered for some time to be impossible, as it seems to require first finding the general solution to Einstein's equations. However, with the use of ideas involved in Dittrich's approximation scheme (built on ideas of Carlo Rovelli) a way to explicitly implement, at least in principle, a reduced phase-space quantization was made viable.

Avshalom Elitzur and Shahar Dolev argue that quantum-mechanical experiments such as the "quantum liar" provide evidence of inconsistent histories, and that spacetime itself may therefore be subject to change affecting entire histories. Elitzur and Dolev also believe that an objective passage of time and relativity can be reconciled and that it would resolve many of the issues with the block universe and the conflict between relativity and quantum mechanics.

One solution to the problem of time proposed by Lee Smolin is that there exists a "thick present" of events, in which two events in the present can be causally related to each other, but in contrast to the block-universe view of time in which all time exists eternally. Marina Cortês and Lee Smolin argue that certain classes of discrete dynamical systems demonstrate time asymmetry and irreversibility, which is consistent with an objective passage of time.
## Weyl time in scale-invariant quantum gravity

Motivated by the Immirzi ambiguity in loop quantum gravity and the near-conformal invariance of the standard model of elementary particles, Charles Wang and co-workers have argued that the problem of time may be related to an underlying scale invariance of gravity–matter systems. Scale invariance has also been proposed to resolve the hierarchy problem of fundamental couplings. As a global continuous symmetry, scale invariance generates a conserved Weyl current according to Noether's theorem. In scale-invariant cosmological models, this Weyl current naturally gives rise to a harmonic time. In the context of loop quantum gravity, Charles Wang et al. suggest that scale invariance may lead to the existence of a quantized time.
## Thermal time hypothesis

The thermal time hypothesis is a possible solution to the problem of time in classical and quantum theory as has been put forward by Carlo Rovelli and Alain Connes. They develop a statistical mechanics model of gravity and characterize thermodynamic time as a vector flow of the statistical state. This thermodynamic time has the common characteristics of time concepts.
w-firewall-physics: A black hole firewall is a hypothetical phenomenon where an observer falling into a black hole encounters high-energy quanta at (or near) the event horizon. The "firewall" phenomenon was proposed in 2012 by physicists Ahmed Almheiri, Donald Marolf, Joseph Polchinski, and James Sully as a possible solution to an apparent inconsistency in black hole complementarity. The proposal is sometimes referred to as the AMPS firewall, an acronym for the names of the authors of the 2012 paper. The potential inconsistency pointed out by AMPS had been pointed out earlier by Samir Mathur who used the argument in favour of the fuzzball proposal. The use of a firewall to resolve this inconsistency remains controversial, with physicists divided as to the solution to the paradox.

According to quantum field theory in curved spacetime, a single emission of Hawking radiation involves two mutually entangled particles. The outgoing particle escapes and is emitted as a quantum of Hawking radiation; the infalling particle is swallowed by the black hole. Assume that a black hole formed a finite time in the past and will fully evaporate away in some finite time in the future. Then, it will only emit a finite amount of information encoded within its Hawking radiation. For an old black hole that has crossed the half-way point of evaporation, general arguments from quantum-information theory by Page and Lubkin suggest that the new Hawking radiation must be entangled with the old Hawking radiation. However, since the new Hawking radiation must also be entangled with degrees of freedom behind the horizon, this creates a paradox: a principle called "monogamy of entanglement" requires that, like any quantum system, the outgoing particle cannot be fully entangled with two independent systems at the same time; yet here the outgoing particle appears to be entangled with both the infalling particle and, independently, with past Hawking radiation.

AMPS initially argued that to resolve the paradox physicists may eventually be forced to give up one of three time-tested principles: Einstein's equivalence principle, unitarity, or existing quantum field theory. However, it is now accepted that an additional tacit assumption in the monogamy paradox was that of locality. A common view is that theories of quantum gravity do not obey exact locality, which leads to a resolution of the paradox. On the other hand, some physicists argue that such violations of locality cannot resolve the paradox.

Some scientists suggest that the entanglement must somehow get immediately broken between the infalling particle and the outgoing particle. Removing the cross-horizon entanglement required for the freely falling vacuum generally turns the horizon into an excited state. Because near-horizon modes can have arbitrarily short wavelengths and large local frequencies, those excitations may carry an extremely large local energy density. This resolution requires a violation of Einstein's equivalence principle, which states that free-falling is indistinguishable from floating in empty space. This violation has been characterized as "outrageous"; theoretical physicist Raphael Bousso has complained that "a firewall simply can't appear in empty space, any more than a brick wall can suddenly appear in an empty field and smack you in the face."

Some scientists suggest that there is in fact no entanglement between the emitted particle and previous Hawking radiation. This resolution would require black hole information loss, a controversial violation of unitarity.

Others, such as Steve Giddings, suggest modifying quantum field theory so that entanglement would be gradually lost as the outgoing and infalling particles separate, resulting in a more gradual release of energy inside the black hole, and consequently no firewall.

The Papadodimas–Raju proposal posited that the interior of the black hole was described by the same degrees of freedom as the Hawking radiation. This resolves the monogamy paradox by identifying the two systems that the late Hawking radiation is entangled with. Since, in this proposal, these systems are the same, there is no contradiction with the monogamy of entanglement. Along similar lines, Juan Maldacena and Leonard Susskind suggested in the ER equals EPR proposal that the outgoing and infalling particles are somehow connected by wormholes, and therefore are not independent systems.

The fuzzball picture resolves the dilemma by replacing the 'no-hair' vacuum with a stringy quantum state, thus explicitly coupling any outgoing Hawking radiation with the formation history of the black hole.

Stephen Hawking received widespread mainstream media coverage in January 2014 with an informal proposal to replace the event horizon of a black hole with an "apparent horizon" where infalling matter is suspended and then released; however, some scientists have expressed confusion about what precisely is being proposed and how the proposal would solve the paradox.

The firewall would exist at the black hole's event horizon, and would be invisible to observers outside the event horizon. Matter passing through the event horizon into the black hole would immediately be "burned to a crisp" by an arbitrarily hot "seething maelstrom of particles" at the firewall.

In a merger of two black holes, the characteristics of a firewall (if any) may leave a mark on the outgoing gravitational radiation as "echoes" when waves bounce in the vicinity of the fuzzy event horizon. The expected quantity of such echoes is theoretically unclear, as physicists don't currently have a good physical model of firewalls. In 2016, cosmologist Niayesh Afshordi and others argued there were tentative signs of some such echo in the data from the first black hole merger detected by LIGO; more recent work has argued there is no statistically significant evidence for such echoes in the data.
w-swampland-physics: In physics, the term swampland refers to effective low-energy physical theories which are not compatible with quantum gravity. This is in contrast with the so-called "string theory landscape" that are known to be compatible with string theory, which is hypothesized to be a consistent quantum theory of gravity. In other words, the Swampland is the set of consistent-looking theories with no consistent ultraviolet completion with the addition of gravity.

Developments in string theory also suggest that the string theory landscape of false vacuum is vast, so it is natural to ask if the landscape is as vast as allowed by anomaly-free effective field theories. The Swampland program aims to delineate the theories of quantum gravity by identifying the universal principles shared among all theories compatible with gravitational UV completion. The program was initiated by Cumrun Vafa who argued that string theory suggests that the Swampland is in fact much larger than the string theory landscape.

Quantum gravity differs from quantum field theory in several key ways, including locality and UV/IR decoupling. In quantum gravity, a local structure of observables is emergent rather than fundamental. A concrete example of the emergence of locality is AdS/CFT, where the local quantum field theory description in bulk is only an approximation that emerges within certain limits of the theory. Moreover, in quantum gravity, it is believed that different spacetime topologies can contribute to the gravitational path integral, which suggests that spacetime emerges due to one saddle being more dominant. Moreover, in quantum gravity, UV and IR are closely related. This connection is manifested in black hole thermodynamics, where a semiclassical IR theory calculates the black hole entropy, which captures the density of gravitational UV states known as black holes. In addition to general arguments based on black hole physics, developments in string theory also suggests that there are universal principles shared among all the theories in the string landscape.

The swampland conjectures are a set of conjectured criteria for theories in the quantum gravity landscape. The criteria are often motivated by black hole physics, universal patterns in string theory, and non-trivial self-consistencies among each other.
## No global symmetry conjecture

The no global symmetry conjecture states that any symmetry in quantum gravity is either broken or gauged. In other words, there are no accidental symmetries in quantum gravity. The original motivation for the conjecture goes back to black holes. Hawking radiation of a generic black hole is only sensitive to charges that can be measured outside of the black hole, which are charges under gauge symmetries. Therefore, it is believed that the process of black hole formation and evaporation violates any conservation which is not protected by gauge symmetry. The no global symmetry conjecture can also be derived from AdS/CFT correspondence in AdS.
## Generalization to higher-form symmetries

The modern understanding of global and gauge symmetries allows for a natural generalization of the no-global symmetry conjectures to higher-form symmetries. A conventional symmetry (0-form symmetry) is a map that acts on point-like operators. For example, a free complex scalar field has a U(1) symmetry which acts on the operator as where alpha is a constant. One can use the symmetry to associate an operator to any symmetry element g and codimension-1 hypersurface sigma such that maps any charged local operator such as to g if the point x is enclosed (or linked) by sigma. By definition, the action of the operator does not change by a continuous deformation of sigma as long as sigma does not hit a charged operator. Due to this feature, the operator is called a topological operator. If the algebra governing the fusion of the symmetry operators has an element without an inverse, the corresponding symmetry is called a non-invertible symmetry.

The above definitions can be generalized to higher dimensional charged operators. A collection of codimension-(p+1) topological operators which act non-trivially on dimension-p operators and are closed under fusion is called a p-form symmetry. Compactification of a higher dimensional theory with a p-form symmetry on a p-dimensional torus can map the higher form symmetry to a 0-form symmetry in the lower dimensional theory. Therefore, it is believed that higher-form global symmetries are also excluded from quantum gravity.
Note that gauge symmetry does not satisfy this definition since, in the process of gauging, any local charged operator is excluded from the physical spectrum.
## Cobordism conjecture

Global symmetries are closely connected to conservation laws. The no-global symmetry conjecture essentially states that any conservation law that is not protected by a gauge symmetry can be violated via a dynamical process. This intuition leads to the cobordism conjecture.

Cobordism conjecture states that there must be a dynamical process which connects the two backgrounds to each other. In other words, there must exist a domain wall in the lower-dimensional theory which separates the two backgrounds. This resembles the idea of cobordism in mathematics, which interpolates between two manifolds by connecting them using a higher dimensional manifold.
## Completeness of spectrum hypothesis

The completeness of spectrum hypothesis conjectures that in quantum gravity, the spectrum of charges under any gauge symmetry is completely realized. This conjecture is universally satisfied in string theory, but is also motivated by black hole physics. The entropy of charged black holes is non-zero. Since the exponential of entropy counts the number of states, the non-zero entropy of black holes suggests that for sufficiently high charges, any charge is realized by at least one black hole state.
## Relation to no-global symmetry conjecture
The completeness of spectrum hypothesis is closely related to the no global symmetry conjecture.

Consider a U(1) gauge symmetry. In the absence of charged particles, the theory has a 1-form global symmetry (ℝ,+). For any number c∈ℝ and any codimension 2 surface sigma, the symmetry operator multiplies a Wilson line that links with sigma by eicn, where the charge associated with the Wilson line is n units of the fundamental charge.

In the presence of charged particles, Wilson lines can break up. Suppose there is a charged particle with charge k, the Wilson lines can change their charges for multiples of k. Therefore, some of the symmetry operators are no longer well-defined.,k/k} give rise to well defined symmetry operators. Therefore, a ℤk part of the global symmetry survives. To avoid any global symmetry, k must be 1 which means all charges appear in the spectrum.

The above argument can be generalized to discrete and higher-dimensional symmetries. The completeness of spectrum follows from the absence of generalized global symmetry which also includes non-invertible symmetries.
## Weak gravity conjecture

The weak gravity conjecture (WGC) is a conjecture regarding the strength gravity can have in a theory of quantum gravity relative to the gauge forces in that theory. It roughly states that gravity should be the weakest force in any consistent theory of quantum gravity.
## Original conjecture

The weak gravity conjecture postulates that every black hole must decay unless it is protected by supersymmetry. Suppose there is a U(1) gauge symmetry, there is an upper bound on the charge of the black holes with a given mass. The black holes that saturate that bound are extremal black holes. The extremal black holes have zero Hawking temperature. However, whether or not a black hole with a charge and a mass that exactly satisfies the extremality condition exists depends on the quantum theory. But given the high entropy of the large extremal black holes, there must exist many states with charges and masses that are arbitrarily close to the extremality condition. Suppose the black hole emits a particle with charge q and mass m.
## Mild version

Given that black holes are the natural extension of particles beyond a certain mass, it is natural to assume that there must also be black holes with a charge-to-mass ratio that is greater than that of very large black holes. In other words, the correction to the extremality condition must be such that
## Higher dimensional generalization

Weak gravity conjecture can be generalized to higher-form gauge symmetries. The generalization postulates that for any higher-form gauge symmetry, there exists a brane which has a charge-to-mass ratio that exceeds the charge-to-mass ratio of the extremal branes.
## Distance conjecture

String dualities have played a crucial role in developing the modern understanding of string theory by providing a non-perturbative window into UV physics. In string theory, when one takes the vacuum expectation values of the scalar fields of a theory to a certain limit, a dual description always emerges. An example of this is T-duality, where there are two dual descriptions to understand a string theory with an internal geometry of a circle. However, each perturbative description becomes valid in a different regime of the parameter space. The circle's radius manifests itself as a scalar field in the lower dimensional theory. If one takes the value of this scalar field to infinity, the resulting theory can be described by the original higher dimensional theory. The new description includes a tower of light states corresponding to the Kaluza-Klein (KK) particles. On the other hand, if we take the size of the circle to zero, the strings that wind around the circle will become light. T-duality is the statement that there exists an alternative description which captures these light winding states as KK particles. Note that in the absence of a string, there is no reason to believe any states should become light in the limit where the size of the circle goes to zero. Distance conjecture quantifies the above observation and states that it must happen at any infinite distance limit of the parameter space.
## Original conjecture

If one takes the vacuum expectation value of the scalar fields to infinity, there exists a tower of light and weakly coupled states whose mass in Planck units goes to zero. Moreover, there is a universal dimension-dependent lower bound on lambda.
The canonical distance between two points in the target space for scalar expectations values (moduli space) is measured using the canonical metric G, which is defined by the kinetic term in action.
## Emergent string conjecture

A stronger version of the original distance conjecture additionally postulates that the lightest tower of states at any infinite distance limit is either a KK tower or a string tower. In other words, the leading tower of states can either be understood via dimensional reduction of a higher dimensional theory (just like the example provided above) or as excitations of a weakly coupled string.
This conjecture is often further strengthened by imposing the string to be a fundamental string.

w-inhomogeneous-cosmology: An inhomogeneous cosmology is a physical cosmological theory (an astronomical model of the physical universe's origin and evolution) which, unlike the dominant cosmological concordance model, postulates that inhomogeneities in the distribution of matter across the universe affect local gravitational forces (that is at the galactic level) enough to skew our view of the Universe. When the universe began, matter was distributed homogeneously, but over billions of years, galaxies, clusters of galaxies, and superclusters coalesced. Einstein's theory of general relativity states that they warp the space-time around them.

While the concordance model acknowledges this fact, it assumes that such inhomogeneities are not sufficient to affect large-scale averages of gravity observations. Two studies claimed in 1998-1999 that high redshift supernovae were further away than the distance predicted by calculations. It was suggested that the expansion of the universe was accelerating, and dark energy, a repulsive energy inherent in space, was proposed as an explanation. Dark energy became widely accepted, but remains unexplained. Inhomogeneous cosmology falls into the class of models that might not require dark energy.

Inhomogeneous cosmologies assume that the backreactions of denser structures and those of empty voids on space-time are significant. When not neglected, they distort understanding of time and observations of distant objects. Burchert's equations in 1997 and 2000 derive from general relativity, but allow for the inclusion of local gravitational variations. Alternative models were proposed under which the acceleration of the universe was a misinterpretation of astronomical observations and in which dark energy is unnecessary. For example, in 2007, David Wiltshire proposed a model (timescape cosmology) in which backreactions caused time to run more slowly or, in voids, more quickly, thus leading supernovae observed in 1998 to be thought to be further away than they were. Timescape cosmology may also imply that the expansion of the universe is in fact slowing.
## Standard cosmological model

The conflict between the two cosmologies derives from the inflexibility of Einstein's theory of general relativity, which shows how gravity is formed by the interaction of matter, space, and time. Physicist John Wheeler famously summed up the theory's essence as "Matter tells space how to curve; space tells matter how to move." However, in order to build a workable cosmological model, all of the terms on both sides of Einstein's equations must be balanced: on one side, matter (that is all the things that warp time and space); on the other, the curvature of the universe and the speed at which space-time is expanding. In short, a model requires a particular amount of matter in order to produce particular curvatures and expansion rates.

In terms of matter, all modern cosmologies are founded on the cosmological principle, which states that whichever direction we look from Earth, the universe is basically the same: homogeneous and isotropic (uniform in all dimensions). This principle grew out of Copernicus's assertion that there were no special observers in the universe and nothing special about the Earth's location in the universe (that is Earth was not the center of the universe, as previously thought). Since the publication of general relativity in 1915, this homogeneity and isotropy have greatly simplified the process of devising cosmological models.

In terms of the curvature of space-time and the shape of the universe, it can theoretically be closed (positive curvature, or space-time folding in itself as though on a four-dimensional sphere's surface), open (negative curvature, with space-time folding outward), or flat (zero curvature, like the surface of a "flat" four-dimensional piece of paper).

The first real difficulty came with regards to expansion, for in 1915, as previously, the universe was assumed to be static, neither expanding nor contracting. All of Einstein's solutions to his equations in general relativity, however, predicted a dynamic universe. Therefore, in order to make his equations consistent with the apparently static universe, he added a cosmological constant, a term representing some unexplained extra energy. But when in the late 1920s Georges Lemaître's and Edwin Hubble's observations proved Alexander Friedmann's notion (derived from general relativity) that the universe was expanding, the cosmological constant became unnecessary, Einstein calling it "my greatest blunder."

With this term gone from the equation, others derived the Friedmann-Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) solution to describe such an expanding universe — a solution built on the assumption of a flat, isotropic, homogeneous universe. The FLRW model became the foundation of the standard model of a universe created by the Big Bang, and further observational evidence has helped to refine it. For example, a smooth, mostly homogeneous, and (at least when it was almost 400,000 years old) flat universe seemed to be confirmed by data from the cosmic microwave background (CMB). And after galaxies and clusters of galaxies were found in the 1970s, mainly by Vera Rubin, to be rotating faster than they should without flying apart, the existence of dark matter seemed also proven, confirming its inference by Jacobus Kapteyn, Jan Oort, and Fritz Zwicky in the 1920s and 1930s and demonstrating the flexibility of the standard model. Dark matter is believed to make up roughly 23 percent of the energy density of the universe.
## Dark energy

Another observation in 1998 seemed to complicate the situation further: two separate studies found distant supernovae to be fainter than expected in a steadily expanding universe; that is, they were not merely moving away from the earth but accelerating. The universe's expansion was calculated to have been accelerating since approximately 5 billion years ago. Given the gravitation braking effect that all the matter of the universe should have had on this expansion, a variation of Einstein's cosmological constant was reintroduced to represent an energy inherent in space, balancing the equations for a flat, accelerating universe. It also gave Einstein's cosmological constant new meaning, for by reintroducing it into the equation to represent dark energy, a flat universe expanding ever faster can be reproduced.

Although the nature of this energy has yet to be adequately explained, it makes up almost 70 percent of the energy density of the universe in the concordance model. And thus, when including dark matter, almost 95 percent of the universe's energy density is explained by phenomena that have been inferred but not entirely explained nor directly observed. Most cosmologists still accept the concordance model, although science journalist Anil Ananthaswamy calls this agreement a "wobbly orthodoxy."
## Inhomogeneous universe

While the universe began with homogeneously distributed matter, enormous structures have since coalesced over billions of years: hundreds of billions of stars inside of galaxies, clusters of galaxies, superclusters, and vast filaments of matter. These denser regions and the voids between them must, under general relativity, have some effect, as matter dictates how space-time curves. So the extra mass of galaxies and galaxy clusters (and dark matter, should particles of it ever be directly detected) must cause nearby space-time to curve more positively, and voids should have the opposite effect, causing space-time around them to take on negative curvatures. The question is whether these effects, called backreactions, are negligible or together comprise enough to change the universe's geometry. Most scientists have assumed that they are negligible, but this has partly been because there has been no way to average space-time geometry in Einstein's equations.

In 2000, a set of new equations—now referred to as the set of Buchert equations—based on general relativity was published by cosmologist Thomas Buchert of the École Normale Supérieure in Lyon, France, which allow the effects of a non-uniform distribution of matter to be taken into account but still allow the behavior of the universe to be averaged. Thus, models based on a lumpy, inhomogeneous distribution of matter could now be devised. "There is no dark energy, as far as I'm concerned," Buchert told New Scientist in 2016. "In ten years' time, dark energy is gone." In the same article, cosmologist Syksy Räsänen said, "It's not been established beyond reasonable doubt that dark energy exists. But I'd never say that it has been established that dark energy does not exist." He also told the magazine that the question of whether backreactions are negligible in cosmology "has not been satisfactorily answered."
## Inhomogeneous cosmology

Inhomogeneous cosmology in the most general sense (assuming a totally inhomogeneous universe) is modeling the universe as a whole with the spacetime which does not possess any spacetime symmetries. Typically considered cosmological spacetimes have either the maximal symmetry, which comprises three translational symmetries and three rotational symmetries (homogeneity and isotropy with respect to every point of spacetime), the translational symmetry only (homogeneous models), or the rotational symmetry only (spherically symmetric models). Models with fewer symmetries (for example axisymmetric) are also considered as symmetric. However, it is common to call spherically symmetric models or non-homogeneous models as inhomogeneous. In inhomogeneous cosmology, the large-scale structure of the universe is modeled by exact solutions of the Einstein field equations (that is non-perturbatively), unlike cosmological perturbation theory, which is study of the universe that takes structure formation (galaxies, galaxy clusters, the cosmic web) into account but in a perturbative way.

Inhomogeneous cosmology usually includes the study of structure in the Universe by means of exact solutions of Einstein's field equations (that is metrics) or by spatial or spacetime averaging methods. Such models are not homogeneous, but may allow effects which can be interpreted as dark energy, or can lead to cosmological structures such as voids or galaxy clusters.
## Perturbative approach

Perturbation theory, which deals with small perturbations from for example a homogeneous metric, only holds as long as the perturbations are not too large, and N-body simulations use Newtonian gravity which is only a good approximation when speeds are low and gravitational fields are weak.
## Non-perturbative approach

Work towards a non-perturbative approach includes the Relativistic Zel'dovich Approximation. As of 2016, Thomas Buchert, George Ellis, Edward Kolb, and their colleagues judged that if the universe is described by cosmic variables in a backreaction scheme that includes coarse-graining and averaging, then whether dark energy is an artifact of the traditional way of using the Einstein equation remains an unanswered question.
## Exact solutions

The first historical examples of inhomogeneous (though spherically symmetric) solutions are the Lemaître–Tolman metric (or LTB model - Lemaître–Tolman-Bondi). The Stephani metric can be spherically symmetric or totally inhomogeneous. Other examples are the Szekeres metric, Szafron metric, Barnes metric, Kustaanheimo-Qvist metric, and Senovilla metric. The Bianchi metrics as given in the Bianchi classification and Kantowski-Sachs metrics are homogeneous.
## Averaging methods

The simplest averaging approach is the scalar averaging approach, leading to the kinematical backreaction and mean 3-Ricci curvature functionals. Buchert's equations are the most commonly used equations of such averaging methods. The simplest averaging kernels include spheres (cylinders, when viewed with a time component), Gaussians, and hard-momentum cutoffs. The former work well for non-relativistic fluids (dust); the later are more convenient for relativistic fluid calculations (photons and pre-recombination universes).
## Timescape cosmology

In 2007, David L Wiltshire, a professor of theoretical physics at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, argued in the New Journal of Physics that quasilocal variations in gravitational energy had in 1998 given the false conclusion that the expansion of the universe is accelerating. Moreover, due to the equivalence principle, which holds that gravitational and inertial energy are equivalent and thus prevents aspects of gravitational energy from being differentiated at a local level, scientists thus misidentified these aspects as dark energy. This misidentification was the result of presuming an essentially homogeneous universe, as the standard cosmological model does, and not accounting for temporal differences between matter-dense areas and voids. Wiltshire and others argued that if the universe is not only assumed not to be homogeneous but also not flat, models could be devised in which the apparent acceleration of the universe's expansion could be explained otherwise.

One more important step being left out of the standard model, Wiltshire claimed, was the fact that as proven by observation, gravity slows time. Thus, from the perspective of the same observer, a clock will move faster in empty space, which possesses low gravitation, than inside a galaxy, which has much more gravity, and he argued that as large as a 38 percent difference between the time on clocks in the Milky Way galaxy and those floating in a void exists. Thus, unless we can correct for that—timescapes each with different times—our observations of the expansion of space will be, and are, incorrect. Wiltshire claims that the 1998 supernovae observations that led to the conclusion of an expanding universe and dark energy can instead be explained by Buchert's equations if certain strange aspects of general relativity are taken into account. The arguments of Wiltshire have been contested by Ethan Siegel.
## Observational evidence

A 2024 study examining the Pantheon+ Type Ia Supernova dataset conducted a significant test of the Timescape cosmology. By employing a model-independent statistical approach, the researchers found that the Timescape model could account for the observed cosmic acceleration without the need for dark energy. This result suggested that inhomogeneous cosmological models may offer viable alternatives to the standard framework and warranted further exploration to assess their ability to explain other key cosmological phenomena.
o-ov-controversies: Science is often presented as a list of facts, but at its frontier it is a set of arguments. Cosmology is full of them, and they are among the most enjoyable parts of the subject. This section gathers the great controversies and open problems, with original explainers that try to give each side its strongest case, and encyclopaedia articles that go into the details.

It helps to sort the arguments into kinds. Some are tensions between measurements: two good ways of measuring the same thing disagree. The most famous is the Hubble tension. Measure the expansion rate of the universe today using nearby stars and supernovae, and you get about seventy-three kilometres per second per megaparsec. Predict it from the cosmic microwave background, using the standard model, and you get about sixty-seven. The gap has resisted years of scrutiny. Either there is a subtle error somewhere, or the standard model is missing something.

Some are problems that a theory was invented to solve. The horizon problem asks why opposite sides of the sky have the same temperature, when they could never have exchanged heat. The flatness problem asks why space is so precisely flat, when any slight curvature in the beginning should have grown enormously. The magnetic monopole problem asks why we see none of the exotic particles that grand unified theories predict. Inflation was proposed to solve all three, and its supporters regard its success as decisive. Its critics argue that inflation is so flexible that it can fit almost anything, and that it needs its own fine-tuning.

Some are about what the universe is made of. Dark matter has been inferred for decades from the motions of galaxies, the bending of light and the microwave background, yet no dark matter particle has ever been caught in a detector. A minority of researchers argue that gravity itself behaves differently at very low accelerations, an idea called modified Newtonian dynamics, or MOND. It works impressively well for individual galaxies, but struggles with clusters of galaxies and with the cosmic microwave background. Dark energy is even more mysterious. Quantum theory suggests that empty space should have an enormous energy, but the observed value is smaller than the naive prediction by something like a hundred and twenty powers of ten. This is the cosmological constant problem, sometimes called the worst prediction in physics. And there is the asymmetry between matter and antimatter: the laws of physics as we know them treat the two almost equally, so why is there anything left at all?

Some controversies come from surprises in new data. In 2014, the BICEP2 team announced evidence for primordial gravitational waves from inflation, a potential Nobel prize discovery; within a year it was clear that the signal was mostly dust in our own galaxy. It became a lesson in how science corrects itself. Since 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope has found surprisingly bright, massive-looking galaxies very early in cosmic history. Early headlines claimed they broke the Big Bang. The real picture, as it has developed, is subtler and more interesting, involving how efficiently the first galaxies made stars, and how bright young stars and growing black holes can be.

And some arguments shade into philosophy. Why do the constants of nature seem so finely tuned for complex structures, stars and life? Is that a clue to a deeper theory, the result of selection among many universes in a multiverse, or a question without meaning? Can a theory that predicts unobservable universes be scientific? What happens to information that falls into a black hole: is it destroyed, which would break quantum theory, or somehow preserved? And why does time have a direction at all, when the fundamental laws seem not to care which way it runs? The answer seems to lie in the extraordinarily low entropy of the early universe, which only pushes the question back to the beginning.
None of these arguments is settled, which means some of what you hear will age. The explainers here describe the state of play as of late 2026, and say plainly where opinion is divided.
o-c01: How fast is the universe expanding? It sounds like a simple question, and for most of the twentieth century the struggle was simply to get any reliable answer at all. Edwin Hubble's first estimate, in 1929, was about five hundred kilometres per second per megaparsec, meaning that a galaxy a megaparsec away, about three point two six million light years, recedes at five hundred kilometres per second, one twice as far at a thousand, and so on. That figure was far too high, because Hubble's distances were wrong. For decades afterwards, astronomers argued bitterly over whether the true value was about fifty or about a hundred. In 2001, the Hubble Space Telescope Key Project, led by Wendy Freedman, settled on about seventy-two, with an uncertainty of about ten percent. It seemed the argument was over. It was not.

Today there are two main ways to measure the expansion rate, now called the Hubble constant. The first is the distance ladder. You measure the distances to nearby pulsating stars called Cepheids, using the parallax method, which is pure geometry. You then find Cepheids in nearby galaxies that have also hosted a particular kind of exploding star, a type one A supernova, whose peak brightness is very consistent. That calibrates the supernovae, which can then be seen in galaxies hundreds of millions of light years away, far enough that their motion is dominated by cosmic expansion. The team called SH0ES, led by Adam Riess, who shared the Nobel prize for discovering the accelerating expansion, has refined this method for twenty years. Their answer is about seventy-three, with an uncertainty of about one and a half percent.

The second way is to infer the expansion rate from the early universe. The cosmic microwave background contains a ruler of known physical size, the sound horizon, the distance sound waves travelled in the plasma before recombination. Measuring how big that ruler looks on the sky, and assuming the standard Lambda CDM model to describe how the universe evolved since, gives the expansion rate today. The Planck satellite's answer is sixty-seven point four, with an uncertainty below one percent. Independent measurements, from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope and the South Pole Telescope, and from the baryon acoustic oscillation ruler in galaxy surveys combined with the abundance of deuterium, agree with Planck.

Seventy-three against sixty-seven is a difference of about eight percent, and the statistical significance has grown to around five standard deviations, the level at which particle physicists would claim a discovery. That is the Hubble tension.

There are two broad schools of thought. The first says something is wrong with the measurements, most likely somewhere in the distance ladder, because it has many steps. Perhaps Cepheids in crowded fields of distant galaxies look brighter than they are because of blending with nearby stars. Perhaps supernovae in the calibrating galaxies differ subtly from those farther away. The James Webb Space Telescope, with its sharper infrared vision, was expected to settle this. Riess's team used Webb to re-observe Cepheids and found the crowding was not the problem; their value stood. But Wendy Freedman's team, using Webb to measure distances with other kinds of stars, the brightest red giants and a class of carbon-rich stars, found values closer to seventy, which they argue are consistent with Planck within the uncertainties. The two teams have debated vigorously, and as of 2026 the disagreement between them is itself unresolved. Other methods, such as measuring the time delays of lensed quasars or using gravitational waves from merging neutron stars as standard sirens, are not yet precise enough to decide.

The second school says the measurements are right, and the standard model is missing something. Since the problem is a mismatch between the early universe and the late universe, the fix might lie in either. Early-universe fixes include early dark energy: an extra component that briefly boosted the expansion just before recombination, shrinking the sound horizon and raising the inferred value. Other ideas include extra kinds of neutrino-like particles, interacting dark matter, or variations in fundamental constants. The difficulty is that the microwave background is now measured so precisely that most changes that fix the Hubble constant spoil the fit elsewhere. Results from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope in 2025 found no sign of early dark energy. Late-universe fixes, such as dark energy that changes with time, generally do not help much, though the DESI survey's recent hints that dark energy may be evolving have added a new twist.

So the tension stands at a fork. If it is an error, finding it will be a lesson in how hard precision astronomy is. If it is real, it may be the first crack in a model that has explained almost everything for twenty-five years. Either way, it is one of the most closely watched numbers in science.
o-c02: In the 1930s, the Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky noticed that galaxies in the Coma cluster were moving far too fast to be held together by the gravity of the stars he could see. There must, he said, be a great deal of invisible matter. For forty years few took this seriously. Then, in the 1970s, Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured how fast stars and gas orbit in spiral galaxies. If most of a galaxy's mass were in its bright centre, outer stars should orbit more slowly, just as Neptune orbits the Sun more slowly than Mercury. Instead, the orbital speeds stayed flat far out beyond the visible disc. Either galaxies are embedded in vast haloes of unseen matter, or gravity does not behave as Newton and Einstein said.

The mainstream answer is dark matter: a substance with mass that neither emits nor absorbs light. The case for it is not one argument but many, from very different areas. Rotation curves of galaxies. The motions of galaxies in clusters. The temperature of hot gas in clusters, seen in X-rays. Gravitational lensing, where the bending of light by mass shows far more mass than the stars and gas provide. The pattern of peaks in the cosmic microwave background, which requires a component that felt gravity but not the pressure of light, about five times as much as ordinary matter. The amount of ordinary matter fixed by the first three minutes, which is far too little to explain the gravity. And the growth of the cosmic web: without dark matter, the tiny ripples in the microwave background could not have grown into galaxies in the time available. Perhaps most vivid is the Bullet Cluster, two clusters of galaxies that collided. The hot gas, which is most of their ordinary matter, was slowed by the collision and sits in the middle, while lensing shows that most of the mass passed straight through, along with the galaxies. Mass and ordinary matter have been separated, exactly as collisionless dark matter would predict.

The weakness is that nobody has caught a dark matter particle. For decades, the favourite candidate was the weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP, which arose naturally in theories such as supersymmetry. Detectors of growing size, now holding tonnes of liquid xenon deep underground, have found nothing; they are now reaching the level where neutrinos from the Sun begin to dominate. The Large Hadron Collider has found no supersymmetric particles. Attention has turned to other candidates: axions, very light particles that could form a kind of wave-like dark matter; sterile neutrinos; primordial black holes; or a whole hidden sector of particles with their own forces.

The alternative was proposed in 1983 by the Israeli physicist Mordehai Milgrom: modified Newtonian dynamics, or MOND. Milgrom suggested that at extremely low accelerations, below about a ten-billionth of a metre per second per second, far weaker than anything in the solar system, gravity becomes stronger than Newton's law predicts. With one new constant, MOND predicts the rotation curves of hundreds of galaxies remarkably well, often better than dark matter models, which need to adjust the halo for each galaxy. It also explains a striking regularity, the baryonic Tully Fisher relation: the rotation speed of a galaxy is tightly linked to its total amount of ordinary matter, with very little scatter. Supporters of MOND, such as Stacy McGaugh, argue that this regularity is a clue that dark matter models explain only after the fact.

MOND's problems arise on bigger scales. In clusters of galaxies, MOND still needs some unseen mass, perhaps neutrinos, to explain the observations. The Bullet Cluster is hard to explain without something that behaves like dark matter. And above all, MOND as Milgrom formulated it is not a complete theory consistent with relativity. Relativistic versions have been built, but they have struggled to reproduce the cosmic microwave background as well as dark matter does. In 2017, the detection of gravitational waves and light from merging neutron stars arriving at almost exactly the same time ruled out many of those versions, which predicted the two would travel differently. In 2024, a study of very wide pairs of stars in our galaxy, measured by the Gaia satellite, became a battleground: some analyses claimed MOND-like effects, while a careful study led by Indranil Banik, himself a MOND researcher, found the data strongly favoured ordinary Newtonian gravity.

Where does that leave things? Most cosmologists regard dark matter as overwhelmingly supported, because it explains so many independent observations with a single idea, while acknowledging that we do not know what it is. A minority argue that MOND's success with galaxies reveals something deep that dark matter has not explained. Some researchers explore hybrids, in which dark matter behaves like a superfluid inside galaxies and mimics MOND. The question will be settled either by detecting dark matter directly, or by an observation that one side cannot accommodate.
o-c03: In February 2017, the magazine Scientific American published an article by three physicists, Anna Ijjas, Paul Steinhardt and Abraham Loeb, titled Pop Goes the Universe. It argued that cosmic inflation, the leading theory of the very early universe, was in trouble, and perhaps not even testable science. The response was swift. A letter signed by thirty-three prominent physicists, including Alan Guth, Andrei Linde, Stephen Hawking, and several Nobel laureates, rejected the critique in the strongest terms. It was a rare public row at the top of cosmology, and it is worth understanding both sides.

The case for inflation begins with what it was invented to explain. The universe is extraordinarily smooth on large scales, and space is extraordinarily flat. Without inflation, both facts require the initial conditions to be tuned with astonishing precision. Inflation produces them naturally: a short burst of exponential expansion smooths and flattens whatever came before. But the real strength of inflation, its supporters say, lies in predictions made before the data arrived. Inflation predicted that the primordial fluctuations should be almost, but not exactly, the same strength on all scales, slightly stronger on large scales. It predicted they should follow bell-curve statistics, be present even on scales larger than the horizon at recombination, and affect matter and radiation together. All of these have been confirmed, most precisely by the Planck satellite. The tilt of the spectrum, measured at about three and a half percent, is a particularly striking success: before inflation, there was no reason to expect it. Supporters argue that this is exactly how science should work: a theory proposed to solve one set of problems made new predictions that were then confirmed.

The critics make several points. The first is about flexibility. There are hundreds of models of inflation, with different fields and potential energy shapes. Critics argue that, between them, they can fit almost any outcome, so that the success of some models is not a success for the idea itself. When the simplest models were disfavoured by the absence of primordial gravitational waves, supporters simply moved to other models. A theory that can always be adjusted, critics say, is not being tested. Supporters reply that every specific model makes sharp predictions, that the data has indeed ruled out large classes of models, and that a framework containing many models is normal in physics, as with quantum field theory itself.

The second criticism is about initial conditions. Inflation was meant to make the universe's initial conditions unimportant, but it needs a patch of space that is already fairly smooth for inflation to start. Is that any more natural than starting with a smooth universe? Supporters argue that, in many models, inflation can start from a wide range of conditions, and computer simulations have shown it to be robust; critics dispute how general these results are.

The third and deepest criticism is the multiverse. In most models, inflation, once started, never stops everywhere. Quantum fluctuations keep some regions inflating, while others, like ours, stop and become hot Big Bang universes. This is eternal inflation, and it produces an infinite number of bubble universes, possibly with different laws of physics. In such a multiverse, critics argue, anything that can happen happens infinitely often, so predictions become a matter of comparing infinities, the so-called measure problem, which has no agreed solution. Steinhardt, one of the founders of inflation, now argues that this makes inflation unfalsifiable. Supporters reply that the measure problem is a genuine but separate puzzle, and that the predictions for our own bubble remain testable regardless.

Critics also point to alternatives. Steinhardt and others have developed bouncing cosmologies, in which a slow contraction before a bounce smooths and flattens the universe without inflation, and generates fluctuations in a different way. A key difference is that these models predict essentially no primordial gravitational waves, while many inflation models predict some.

That gives the controversy a possible resolution. If experiments such as the Simons Observatory, BICEP and, later, LiteBIRD detect the twisting B mode pattern from primordial gravitational waves, it would be a powerful confirmation of inflation, and would reveal the energy at which it happened. A null result would not kill inflation, since some models predict signals too weak to see, but it would shrink the space of simple models and strengthen the case of the critics. Many cosmologists today regard inflation as the best available explanation, well supported but not proven, and the debate as a healthy one about how much we really know about the first instants.
o-c04: The word multiverse is used for several different ideas, and much of the argument about it comes from mixing them up. So it is worth separating them first.

The simplest version barely deserves the name. If space is infinite, as it may well be, then the universe extends far beyond the part we can see, our observable universe, which is limited by how far light has travelled since the beginning. Beyond our horizon there would be countless other regions, each as large as ours, with the same laws of physics but different arrangements of matter. Some physicists call these other regions other universes, but they are really just far-off parts of the same universe. Almost every cosmologist accepts that this is possible; the debate is about whether space is truly infinite.

The second version comes from eternal inflation. In most models of inflation, the process never stops everywhere at once. Some regions stop inflating and become hot Big Bang universes, like bubbles in a boiling liquid, while the space between them keeps inflating, creating more bubbles forever. Each bubble is causally disconnected from the others. If the field that drives inflation can settle into different states, the bubbles might have different physical properties.

The third version adds string theory. String theory, our leading candidate for a theory of quantum gravity, seems to allow an enormous number of possible vacuum states, perhaps ten to the five hundred or more, each corresponding to a different set of particles, forces and constants. This collection is called the string landscape. Combined with eternal inflation, which could populate every possible state somewhere, it leads to a multiverse in which the laws of physics themselves vary from bubble to bubble.

There are other versions too. The many worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, proposed by Hugh Everett in 1957, says that every quantum measurement splits reality into branches, all equally real. Max Tegmark has proposed that every mathematically consistent structure exists as a universe. And cyclic models produce a sequence of universes in time rather than space.

Now the argument. Supporters of the inflationary and landscape multiverse, such as Andrei Linde, Alexander Vilenkin, Leonard Susskind and, in a different form, Max Tegmark, make two main points. First, the multiverse is not a theory in itself, but a prediction of theories, inflation and string theory, that are motivated by other evidence. If those theories are right, and they make the multiverse inevitable, then refusing to take it seriously would be like refusing to believe in parts of the Earth you have not visited. Second, a multiverse would explain one of the biggest puzzles in physics: why the constants of nature, especially the tiny value of dark energy, seem finely tuned to allow galaxies, stars and life. In a multiverse with many different values, observers will inevitably find themselves in the rare bubbles where conditions allow observers. In 1987, Steven Weinberg used this reasoning to predict that the cosmological constant should be small but not zero, a decade before dark energy was discovered. Supporters see that as a genuine scientific success.

Critics, including George Ellis, Paul Steinhardt, Sabine Hossenfelder and Peter Woit, argue that a theory predicting unobservable universes cannot be tested, and so is not science but metaphysics. If any observation can be explained by saying we happen to live in a bubble where things are that way, then the theory explains everything and therefore nothing. In 2014, Ellis and Joseph Silk wrote a widely read article in Nature warning that some physicists were proposing to weaken the requirement that theories be testable, and calling on scientists to defend the integrity of physics. Critics also note the measure problem: in an infinite multiverse, there are infinitely many examples of every possibility, so calculating probabilities requires choosing how to count infinities, and different choices give different answers.

Is there any way to test it? Some physicists have proposed that our bubble universe might have collided with a neighbour early on, leaving a circular imprint in the cosmic microwave background. Searches have found nothing convincing so far, though they have set limits. Others argue that if our universe began inside a bubble, space should have a very slight negative curvature, a prediction that future measurements might check. And the theories that predict the multiverse, inflation and string theory, can in principle be tested in other ways; if they gain strong support, belief in the multiverse would follow. A null result would not disprove it, but would remove its motivation.

The multiverse debate is, in the end, partly about what science is. Supporters argue that science has always expanded to include things we cannot directly see, such as atoms or the interior of the Sun, when good theories demand them. Critics answer that those things were eventually tested directly, while other universes may never be. Both sides agree on one thing: it is among the most profound questions human beings have ever asked.
o-c05: On the seventeenth of March 2014, at a packed press conference at the Harvard Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, a team of astronomers announced what seemed to be the discovery of the century. Using a telescope called BICEP2 at the South Pole, they had detected a faint twisting pattern in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, the signature, they said, of gravitational waves created during cosmic inflation, a trillionth of a trillionth of a trillionth of a second after the beginning. A video went around the world of Andrei Linde, one of inflation's founders, opening his front door to find a colleague who told him the news; he and his wife were visibly moved. Newspapers spoke of a Nobel prize. Within a year, the claim had collapsed. The story of BICEP2 is a story about how hard cosmology is, and how science corrects itself.

First, the science. Light from the microwave background is slightly polarised, meaning its waves vibrate more in some directions than others. The polarisation pattern on the sky can be split into two kinds. One, called E modes, has no twist, like the lines radiating from a point or forming circles around it, and is produced by the ordinary density variations of the early universe; it was first detected in 2002. The other, B modes, has a twist, like a pinwheel. On large scales, the only way the early universe could make primordial B modes is through gravitational waves stretching and squeezing space during the era of recombination. And the only plausible source of such large-scale gravitational waves is inflation. So B modes would be close to a smoking gun for inflation, and their strength would reveal the energy at which inflation happened.

BICEP2, led by John Kovac, Clem Pryke, Jamie Bock and Chao-Lin Kuo, observed a small, clean patch of southern sky for three years. They found B modes, far stronger than many expected: a ratio of gravitational waves to density fluctuations of about point two. That was surprisingly large, in tension with earlier limits from the Planck satellite, but the team argued that their signal was robust.

The problem was dust. The Milky Way contains tiny grains of dust that are aligned by the galaxy's magnetic field. When they glow in microwaves, their light is polarised, and it can produce B modes too. To tell primordial B modes from dust, you need to observe at several frequencies, because dust glows more strongly at higher frequencies while the microwave background does not. BICEP2 observed at only one frequency. To estimate the dust in their patch, the team used preliminary information, including, controversially, data digitised from a slide shown in a conference talk by the Planck team, which critics argued had been misinterpreted. Within weeks of the announcement, other researchers, including Raphael Flauger and David Spergel, argued that dust could explain much or all of the signal.

The resolution came through cooperation. Planck, which observed the whole sky at many frequencies, published measurements in late 2014 showing that dust in the BICEP2 patch was much stronger than assumed. The BICEP2 and Planck teams then combined their data, and in early 2015 announced that the signal was consistent with dust alone. The evidence for primordial gravitational waves had evaporated.

Was this a scandal? Opinions differ. Critics said the team had rushed to a press conference before peer review, made extraordinary claims on uncertain evidence, and created a media frenzy that damaged public trust. Defenders said the team had been careful with their own data, had been explicit about the dust uncertainty in their paper, and had made their data public so that others could check it. The real lesson, many cosmologists now say, is that the error was quickly found and corrected by the scientific process, which is exactly how science should work. Some also note that the episode led to much closer collaboration between rival teams, and to a far better understanding of galactic dust.

The search continues, with more frequencies and more sensitivity. The BICEP and Keck Array experiments, now with observations at several frequencies and combined with Planck, have pushed the upper limit on the gravitational wave ratio down to about point zero three six, which already rules out several of the simplest inflation models. Newer experiments at the South Pole and in Chile's Atacama Desert, and the planned Japanese LiteBIRD satellite, aim to reach the levels predicted by the most favoured remaining models. If B modes are eventually found, the BICEP2 affair will be remembered as a false dawn before a real discovery. If not, it will be remembered as the moment cosmologists learned just how much a little dust can hide.
o-c06: In July 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope released its first images, and within days astronomers began posting papers claiming the discovery of astonishingly distant galaxies. Some appeared to be seen just two or three hundred million years after the beginning, and, more surprisingly, to be bright and massive, as if they contained as many stars as the Milky Way does today. Headlines followed: Webb breaks cosmology; the Big Bang never happened. A few writers who had always rejected the Big Bang seized on the results. So what actually happened, and what does it mean?

First, the hype had to be separated from the science. The early claims were based on photometry: measuring the brightness of a galaxy through a set of colour filters and estimating its distance from the colours. For very distant galaxies, a key feature is a sharp drop in light at a particular wavelength, caused by hydrogen absorbing ultraviolet light, which the expansion of the universe shifts into the infrared. But other things can mimic that drop, especially dusty galaxies much closer to us, or galaxies with strong emission from glowing gas. Some of the most extreme early candidates were soon shown to be such impostors. One galaxy, thought to be at a redshift of sixteen, turned out to be at about five. The calibration of Webb's instruments was also still being refined in the first weeks.

But not everything went away. When Webb took spectra, which give precise distances, many early galaxies were confirmed. In 2024, the JADES team confirmed a galaxy at a redshift of fourteen point three, seen about two hundred and ninety million years after the beginning, and in 2025 another team confirmed MoM z fourteen, slightly more distant still. These galaxies are remarkably bright. And statistically, Webb has found several times more bright galaxies in the first five hundred million years than most pre-launch models predicted. That is the real puzzle.

Does it break the Big Bang or the standard Lambda CDM model? The mainstream view is no, for an important reason. The standard model makes firm predictions about how many dark matter haloes of each mass exist at each time. Those predictions are based on well understood physics, and they are generous: there are enough dark matter haloes to host the observed galaxies. The question is how efficiently the gas in those haloes turned into stars. In today's universe, galaxies are inefficient; only a small fraction of their gas becomes stars, because exploding stars and growing black holes blow gas out. Models built to match today's galaxies assumed similar inefficiency in the early universe. Webb is telling us that early galaxies were either more efficient, or brighter for their mass.

Several explanations, not mutually exclusive, are being explored. Star formation in the dense early universe may have been more efficient, because gas was denser and feedback had less time to act. Star formation may have been bursty, so that we preferentially see galaxies caught in a brief bright flare. The first stars may have been more massive on average, making each galaxy brighter for its mass; this is called a top-heavy initial mass function. Dust may have been blown out, leaving galaxies unobscured. And some of the light may come not from stars but from growing black holes. Webb has found a surprising population of compact red objects, nicknamed little red dots, that appear to be black holes shrouded in gas, and their nature is a hot topic.

The original claims of impossibly massive galaxies have also softened. Estimating a galaxy's mass from its light depends on assumptions about its stars; with more realistic assumptions, many early galaxies turn out to be less massive than first thought, though still impressive. A small number of reports of very massive, apparently mature galaxies within the first billion years remain challenging, and are being checked.

So the honest summary is this. Webb did find more and brighter early galaxies than expected, and this is forcing astronomers to rethink how the first galaxies formed and grew. It has not broken the Big Bang, which rests on many independent pillars, nor, so far, the standard cosmological model. It may yet reveal something new, about the first stars, black hole seeds, or even dark matter. That is what a great telescope is for.
o-c07: In 1928, the British physicist Paul Dirac wrote down an equation describing the electron that combined quantum mechanics with special relativity. It had a curious feature: it allowed solutions that seemed to describe electrons with negative energy. Dirac eventually concluded that his equation predicted a new particle, identical to the electron but with opposite charge. In 1932, Carl Anderson found it in cosmic rays and named it the positron. Antimatter was real. Every kind of particle, it turned out, has an antiparticle with the same mass and opposite charges. When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate into energy. And in the laboratory, whenever energy is turned into matter, particles and antiparticles are created in equal numbers.

That symmetry creates one of the deepest puzzles in physics. If the Big Bang made matter and antimatter equally, they should have annihilated almost completely as the universe cooled, leaving a universe filled with light and almost nothing else. Instead, we live in a universe made of matter. Could there be regions made of antimatter elsewhere, antigalaxies? Astronomers have looked. Where matter and antimatter regions met, annihilation would produce gamma rays of a characteristic energy, and no such boundaries have been seen anywhere in the observable universe. The universe seems to be made of matter throughout.

The size of the asymmetry is known precisely. From the first three minutes and the microwave background, there is about one proton or neutron for every one point six billion photons. Tracing back, this means that in the very early universe, for every billion antiquarks there were a billion and one quarks. The billion pairs annihilated; the one survived. Everything we see is made of the survivors.

In 1967, the Soviet physicist Andrei Sakharov, later famous as a dissident and Nobel peace laureate, worked out the three conditions needed to generate such an asymmetry from an initially symmetric start. First, some process must change the number of baryons, the family that includes protons and neutrons. Second, the laws of physics must treat matter and antimatter differently, a property called CP violation; and also, more simply, charge symmetry must be broken. Third, the process must happen out of thermal equilibrium, because in equilibrium any asymmetry would be erased as fast as it was made.

Remarkably, the Standard Model contains all three ingredients in principle. CP violation was discovered in 1964 by James Cronin and Val Fitch, in the decays of particles called kaons, and has since been measured in many other particles. Baryon number can change in the Standard Model through exotic processes called sphalerons, which were active at the high temperatures of the electroweak epoch. And the expansion of the universe provides departures from equilibrium. The problem is quantity. The CP violation in the Standard Model is far too small, by many powers of ten, to explain the observed asymmetry. And, as calculations with the measured Higgs mass show, the electroweak transition was a smooth crossover, not the abrupt, bubbling transition needed for the third condition. The Standard Model fails to make the universe, which means there must be physics beyond it.

What could it be? There are two leading families of ideas. Electroweak baryogenesis adds new particles, perhaps extra Higgs-like fields, that make the electroweak transition violent and add new CP violation. This has the advantage of being testable at colliders, and the disadvantage that the Large Hadron Collider has not seen the required particles, nor have very precise measurements of the electron's shape, which are sensitive to new CP violation, found any. Leptogenesis, proposed by Masataka Fukugita and Tsutomu Yanagida in 1986, says the asymmetry was first created among leptons, through the decays of very heavy neutrinos in the early universe, and then converted to a baryon asymmetry by sphalerons. Leptogenesis is attractive because the same heavy neutrinos could explain why ordinary neutrinos have such tiny masses. Its disadvantage is that the heavy neutrinos would be far too massive to make in any collider.

That is why neutrino experiments matter so much. If neutrinos and antineutrinos oscillate between their types differently, that would show CP violation among leptons, a necessary ingredient of leptogenesis. The Japanese experiment T2 kelvin has reported hints of this, while the American experiment NOvA has been less clear; the two collaborations published a combined analysis in 2025. The next generation, Hyper-Kamiokande and DUNE, should give a definitive answer in the 2030s. Experiments searching for an extremely rare process called neutrinoless double beta decay would show whether neutrinos are their own antiparticles, another key part of the story.

Other ideas exist: baryogenesis through the decay of the inflaton, through grand unified theories, or through scalar fields in supersymmetry. None has been confirmed. So the answer to the question why there is something rather than nothing is, at present, honestly unknown. But physicists know exactly what kind of answer they are looking for, and the experiments that may find it are being built.
o-c08: In 1998, two teams of astronomers, the Supernova Cosmology Project led by Saul Perlmutter and the High-Z Supernova Search Team led by Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess, announced a result neither had expected. Distant exploding stars of a particular type were fainter than they should be if the expansion of the universe were slowing down, as everyone assumed it must be under gravity. The expansion, they concluded, is accelerating. The three leaders shared the Nobel prize in 2011. The cause of the acceleration was given a name, dark energy, which is really a label for our ignorance. It makes up about seventy percent of the energy of the universe today.

The simplest explanation is one that Einstein had invented and then abandoned: the cosmological constant. In general relativity, it is perfectly legitimate to add a constant energy belonging to space itself. Such an energy has a strange property. As space expands, the amount of it in any given volume stays the same, because it belongs to space rather than to things in space. And according to Einstein's equations, an energy that behaves this way has a negative pressure, which causes the expansion to accelerate. So a small cosmological constant explains the observations neatly, and it is the Lambda in the standard Lambda CDM model.

The trouble begins when you ask what the energy of empty space should be. Quantum field theory says that empty space is not empty. Every field has a lowest energy state, its vacuum, in which it still fluctuates, and those fluctuations carry energy. If you add up the energy of all the fluctuations of all the fields, up to the highest energies where we trust our theories, you get an enormous number.
