Estimates vary depending on how you do the calculation, but the naive answer, cut off at the Planck scale, exceeds the observed dark energy by about a hundred and twenty powers of ten: a one followed by a hundred and twenty zeros. More careful estimates reduce the gap to perhaps fifty or sixty powers of ten, still the largest discrepancy between theory and observation in all of physics. This is the cosmological constant problem, and it has been called the worst prediction in the history of physics.

Why doesn't the vacuum energy blow the universe apart? One possibility is that some unknown symmetry or mechanism cancels the contributions almost perfectly, but not quite. Physicists find this hard to accept, because the cancellation would have to be precise to more than a hundred decimal places, and no one has found a mechanism. Supersymmetry, for instance, would cancel some contributions, but not well enough given that supersymmetric particles, if they exist, are heavy. A second possibility is anthropic: in a multiverse with many different values, we necessarily find ourselves where the value is small enough for galaxies to form. As mentioned elsewhere in this library, Steven Weinberg used this argument in 1987 to predict a small non-zero value before it was found. To some this is a triumph; to others it is giving up.

A third possibility is that dark energy is not a constant at all, but a dynamic field, sometimes called quintessence, slowly evolving over cosmic time. Or perhaps gravity itself needs to be modified on cosmic scales. Until recently, all observations were consistent with a pure constant. Then, in April 2024, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, DESI, released its first year of measurements of the baryon acoustic oscillation ruler across cosmic time. Combined with the microwave background and supernova data, the results hinted that dark energy was stronger in the past and is now weakening. In March 2025, DESI's second data release strengthened the hint, to a significance of between about three and four standard deviations, depending on which supernova sample is used.

This is a genuine controversy. Supporters of the result point out that the trend appears in several independent combinations of data. Sceptics note that the significance depends heavily on the supernova samples, which have their own uncertainties; that three or four standard deviations has been reached before by effects that later vanished; and that the preferred model has some odd features, such as dark energy that at some point in the past behaved in a way that is hard to achieve with simple fields. The coming years, with more DESI data, the Euclid space telescope, the Rubin Observatory's supernova survey and the Roman Space Telescope, should settle it.

The stakes are high. If dark energy is a cosmological constant, the universe will expand forever, ever faster, ending in cold emptiness. If it is evolving, the future could be very different, and we would have discovered new physics. And either way, the cosmological constant problem, why the vacuum energy is not enormous, remains one of the biggest unsolved problems in science.
o-c09: Imagine a universe in which the strong nuclear force was a few percent weaker. Deuterium, the stepping stone to every heavier element, might not hold together, and stars could not burn the way they do. Make it a little stronger, and, on some calculations, the protons of the early universe might have fused too readily, leaving little hydrogen for long-lived stars and water. Change the strength of electromagnetism relative to gravity, and stars either burn out too quickly or never ignite. Change the amount of dark energy by a modest factor upwards, and the universe would have flown apart before galaxies could form. Change the size of the early density ripples, and you get either a smooth universe with no galaxies or one where everything collapses into black holes. Physicists have found many such cases, and many argue that the constants of nature appear finely tuned for a universe that can contain complex structures, chemistry and life.

There is a famous example from history. In 1953, Fred Hoyle reasoned that, because carbon exists, and because we are made of it, there must be a particular energy level in the carbon nucleus that allows three helium nuclei to fuse efficiently inside stars. He persuaded experimenters at the California Institute of Technology to look, and they found it, now called the Hoyle state. It is often cited as a successful prediction based on the fact of our own existence, though historians have debated how much Hoyle actually framed it that way.
What should we make of fine-tuning? Broadly, there are four kinds of answer.

The first is that fine-tuning is a clue to deeper physics. Perhaps a future theory will show that the constants could not have been otherwise, as the boiling point of water follows from the properties of molecules. Many physicists hoped string theory would do this. It has not, so far; instead, it seems to allow a vast landscape of possibilities.

The second is the anthropic answer, named and developed by the physicist Brandon Carter in 1973. The weak anthropic principle states something that is almost obvious: we can only observe a universe compatible with our existence. If there were many universes, or many regions with different constants, then observers would inevitably find themselves in the rare ones where observers can exist, and would see fine-tuning even though nothing tuned it. Combined with the multiverse from eternal inflation and the string landscape, this becomes a possible explanation, and some physicists, such as Leonard Susskind and Martin Rees, find it compelling. The prediction of a small cosmological constant by Steven Weinberg in 1987, using this reasoning, is often cited in its favour.

The third answer is sceptical about the premise. Critics, including the physicist Victor Stenger and others, argue that fine-tuning is exaggerated: studies usually vary one constant at a time, while varying several together can open up other habitable combinations; we do not know what forms life could take under different physics; and we cannot calculate probabilities for the constants without knowing how they were selected. Some recent work has explored universes with no weak nuclear force at all and found that they might still form stars and chemistry, though others dispute it.

The fourth answer is theological or philosophical: that fine-tuning points to purpose or design. This is outside science, but it is part of the wider conversation, and some physicists and philosophers take it seriously, while many others reject it.

The strongest scientific criticism of the anthropic approach is that it can become an excuse to stop looking for explanations. If every puzzle can be answered with we happen to live in a universe where it is so, the reasoning goes, then physics has given up its central task. Supporters reply that, if the multiverse is real, anthropic reasoning is simply correct, just as it is correct to say that Earth is at a comfortable distance from the Sun because life could not have arisen on a planet too hot or too cold, not because some law fixed the distance. Between those positions, the debate continues, and it is likely to continue until we have a theory that either fixes the constants or predicts the landscape in a testable way.
o-c10: In 1974, Stephen Hawking made one of the most surprising discoveries in theoretical physics. Applying quantum field theory to the curved space around a black hole, he found that black holes are not completely black. They glow faintly, emitting radiation as if they were hot bodies, with a temperature that is higher the smaller the black hole. A black hole the mass of the Sun would have a temperature of only about sixty billionths of a degree, far colder than the microwave background, so it would actually absorb more than it emits. But in the far future, when the universe is colder still, black holes will slowly evaporate, losing mass until, perhaps after ten to the sixty-seven years for a solar mass black hole, they vanish in a final burst.

Two years later, Hawking pointed out a disturbing consequence. The radiation, according to his calculation, is purely thermal: random, carrying no information about what fell into the black hole. Burn a book and, in principle, all the information in it survives in the smoke, ash and light, scrambled but recoverable. But throw a book into a black hole and let the hole evaporate, and Hawking's calculation says the information is simply gone. That would violate a central principle of quantum mechanics, called unitarity, which says that information is never truly destroyed. Either quantum mechanics is wrong, or something is wrong with Hawking's reasoning about black holes. This is the information paradox.

For two decades, Hawking argued that information is lost, and that quantum mechanics must be modified. Many particle physicists, including Leonard Susskind and Gerard 't Hooft, argued that it must be preserved. In 1997, Hawking and Kip Thorne made a famous bet with John Preskill, who held that information comes out.

A major turning point came in 1997, when Juan Maldacena discovered a precise mathematical correspondence, within string theory, between a kind of universe with gravity and an ordinary quantum theory without gravity living on its boundary. This holographic duality, often called AdS CFT, implied that black hole formation and evaporation could be described entirely by ordinary quantum mechanics, which never loses information. Most theorists took this as strong evidence that information must escape. In 2004, Hawking conceded the bet, giving Preskill an encyclopaedia of baseball, from which, as Hawking joked, information can readily be retrieved.

But conceding was not the same as explaining how. In 1993, Don Page had shown that if information escapes, the entanglement between the black hole and its radiation must follow a particular curve: rising at first, then falling after the black hole has lost about half its mass, a point called the Page time. Hawking's calculation follows only the rising part. In 2012, Ahmed Almheiri, Donald Marolf, Joseph Polchinski and James Sully sharpened the paradox. They argued that if information escapes, then, after the Page time, someone falling into an old black hole would encounter a wall of high energy particles at the event horizon, a firewall, contradicting Einstein's principle that free fall should feel smooth. The firewall argument started a fresh storm of debate.

Then, in 2019, came a breakthrough. Two groups, one including Almheiri, Netta Engelhardt, Marolf and Henry Maxfield, and another led by Geoffrey Penington, showed how to calculate the entanglement of the radiation using a newly understood rule in quantum gravity. Their result reproduced the Page curve: the information does come out. The key ingredient is the idea of islands: regions inside the black hole that, after the Page time, should be counted as part of the radiation outside. Further work showed that the calculation involves contributions called replica wormholes, subtle connections between copies of the spacetime used in the mathematics.

Is the paradox solved? Many theorists believe the question of whether information is preserved has essentially been answered: it is. But the question of how, in terms of what an infalling observer would experience, and how the information gets physically encoded in the radiation, remains open. The calculations work best in simplified models, and it is not certain how they apply to real black holes in our universe. The debate has also become a window into the nature of space itself, with growing evidence that spacetime may emerge from quantum entanglement. The information paradox, which began as a puzzle about evaporating black holes, may turn out to be the key to quantum gravity, and so to the very first moments of the universe.
o-c11: Drop a glass on the floor and it shatters. Run a film of it backwards and you see fragments leaping up and assembling themselves into a glass, and you know immediately that something is wrong. Eggs scramble but never unscramble; milk mixes into coffee but never separates out; we remember the past but not the future. Time seems to have a direction, an arrow. And yet, at the level of individual particles, the fundamental laws of physics, with one tiny exception in the weak force, work equally well forwards and backwards. A film of two billiard balls colliding looks perfectly natural in reverse. So where does the arrow come from?

The standard answer comes from thermodynamics, and in particular from the second law, which says that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Entropy, as Ludwig Boltzmann explained in the 1870s, is a measure of how many microscopic arrangements of a system look the same from the outside. A shattered glass has vastly more possible arrangements than an intact one; milk mixed into coffee has vastly more than milk and coffee separated. So, starting from a special, low-entropy state, random motions will almost certainly lead to higher-entropy states, simply because there are so many more of them. The arrow of time, on this view, is the direction in which entropy increases.

But this explanation contains a hidden assumption. Boltzmann's argument works equally well backwards: if you find a system in a low-entropy state, it is overwhelmingly likely that it was in a higher-entropy state a moment before as well. The only reason entropy increases towards the future, rather than in both directions, is that the past was in an even lower entropy state. Follow that chain back, and you arrive at the beginning of the universe, which must have been in a state of extraordinarily low entropy. Physicist and philosopher David Albert has called this assumption the past hypothesis. Every arrow of time, from breaking glasses to the formation of memories, traces back to it.

That is puzzling, because the early universe looks like it had high entropy. The cosmic microwave background shows a hot, smooth, evenly mixed gas, in thermal equilibrium, which for a gas in a box would be the highest-entropy state possible. The resolution is gravity. For gravitating systems, entropy works the other way: a smooth distribution of matter is low entropy, because gravity can increase entropy by clumping matter into stars, galaxies and, ultimately, black holes, which have colossal entropy. Roger Penrose has estimated that the smoothness of the early universe was so special that, if the initial state were chosen at random, the chance of getting one like ours would be one in ten to the power of ten to the power of a hundred and twenty three, a number so large it is beyond all comparison.

Why was the early universe so special? This is where the controversy lies. Some physicists argue that inflation explains it, because inflation smooths things out. Critics, including Penrose, reply that inflation itself needs a special low-entropy starting state, so it only moves the problem. Sean Carroll and Jennifer Chen have proposed that our Big Bang might be one of many baby universes born from fluctuations in an otherwise high-entropy multiverse, so that the arrow points away from the Big Bang in both directions of time. Penrose's own conformal cyclic cosmology proposes a geometric condition that forces each new aeon to begin smooth. Julian Barbour and colleagues have suggested that the arrow arises from the growth of complexity rather than entropy. Others argue that the low-entropy beginning is simply a brute fact, a boundary condition with no deeper explanation, like the existence of the universe itself.

There is a strange consequence lurking in Boltzmann's original reasoning. If the universe were in equilibrium forever, random fluctuations would occasionally create low-entropy pockets, and small fluctuations are vastly more likely than large ones. It would be far more probable for a single brain, with false memories, to fluctuate into existence than for a whole low-entropy universe. This is the Boltzmann brain problem. Most physicists take it as a sign that any theory predicting vast eternities of equilibrium must be wrong or incomplete, and it is used as a test for cosmological models, including some versions of the far future and the multiverse.

The arrow of time connects the deepest questions about the beginning to the most ordinary experiences of daily life. Every time you remember yesterday rather than tomorrow, you are, in a sense, feeling the low entropy of the Big Bang.
o-c12: It is natural to assume that the Big Bang theory says the universe had a beginning. It does not quite, and whether there was a beginning is one of the most open questions in all of science.

The idea of a beginning seemed to get strong support in the 1960s, when Roger Penrose and Stephen Hawking proved a series of theorems in general relativity. Under reasonable assumptions about matter, they showed, an expanding universe like ours must have begun at a singularity: a moment in the past beyond which the history of matter and light cannot be extended. For a while, it seemed that Einstein's theory itself demanded a beginning of time. In 2003, Arvind Borde, Alan Guth and Alexander Vilenkin proved a related theorem that does not depend on the type of matter: any universe that has, on average, been expanding throughout its history cannot be infinitely old in the past; its history must be incomplete. This applies even to eternal inflation, which may be eternal into the future but not into the past.

However, these theorems all rely on classical general relativity, and everyone agrees that general relativity must fail near the Planck scale, where quantum effects on gravity become important. The singularity theorems tell us that classical physics breaks down; they do not tell us what replaces it. So the question becomes: what does quantum gravity say? And since we do not have a confirmed theory of quantum gravity, the answers are proposals. They fall into roughly three groups.

The first group says there was a genuine beginning, but not a singular one. The most famous is the no-boundary proposal of James Hartle and Stephen Hawking, published in 1983. Using a mathematical technique in which time is treated as if it were a direction of space, they described a universe whose history, near the beginning, rounds off smoothly like the bottom of a bowl. There is no first moment, no edge, and no need for anything to set the initial conditions: asking what happened before the Big Bang, Hawking said, is like asking what lies south of the South Pole. Alexander Vilenkin proposed a different version, in which the universe tunnels quantum mechanically from nothing, where nothing means no space, no time, and no matter. These proposals are mathematically subtle and contested; in 2017, a group of physicists argued that the no-boundary proposal, done carefully, does not produce a smooth universe, prompting replies and refinements. They are also difficult to test, though they make predictions about the kind of inflation that should follow.

The second group says there was no beginning: the universe bounced. In loop quantum cosmology, based on loop quantum gravity, space is made of discrete quanta, and when density approaches the Planck density, gravity becomes repulsive. A contracting universe would then rebound into an expanding one. The Big Bang becomes a Big Bounce, and before it there was a contracting universe, perhaps a mirror image of ours. Cyclic and ekpyrotic models, developed by Paul Steinhardt, Neil Turok and colleagues, describe a sequence of bounces, with long periods of expansion and contraction, possibly repeating forever. In string theory, there are scenarios in which our universe emerged from a previous phase, such as the string gas cosmology of Robert Brandenberger and Cumrun Vafa. Roger Penrose's conformal cyclic cosmology describes an endless sequence of aeons, each beginning with a Big Bang that is the smooth continuation of the infinitely expanded future of the one before. All of these have to address the arrow of time: why, if the universe has been around forever, entropy has not already reached its maximum.

The third group says the question may be ill-formed. If time itself emerges from something more basic, as some approaches to quantum gravity suggest, then asking about a beginning of time might be like asking where a rainbow begins: a question that makes sense at one level of description but not at another. In some approaches, spacetime is built up from quantum entanglement, or from discrete events, and at the deepest level there might be no time at all.

Could we ever know? Some of these proposals make predictions. Bouncing models typically predict essentially no primordial gravitational waves, while many inflationary scenarios predict detectable ones. Some bounce models predict subtle features in the cosmic microwave background on the largest scales, where Planck's measurements show some mild anomalies, though these may be chance. Penrose has claimed to see circular patterns in the microwave background, which he calls Hawking points, as traces of black holes evaporating in the previous aeon; other analyses have not confirmed them. For now, the honest answer is that we do not know whether the universe had a beginning. It is a question that physics has taken from philosophy, and not yet answered.
o-c13: Alongside the big controversies, cosmology has a collection of smaller puzzles: measurements that do not quite fit, effects that might be statistical flukes, or problems that may have mundane explanations. Most will probably turn out to be nothing. But history shows that small anomalies sometimes lead to revolutions, as the slightly misbehaving orbit of Mercury led to general relativity. Here is a tour of the most discussed.

The first is the lithium problem. Big Bang nucleosynthesis predicts the amounts of deuterium, helium and lithium made in the first minutes. Deuterium and helium agree with observations beautifully. But the oldest stars in our galaxy contain about three times less lithium seven than predicted. In 1982, François and Monique Spite discovered that old, metal-poor stars all have about the same amount of lithium, the Spite plateau, which was long assumed to be the primordial value. The possible explanations divide into three. The stars might have destroyed some of their lithium over billions of years, by mixing it down to hot layers where it burns; this is the favourite explanation, but models have trouble destroying the right amount evenly in all stars. The nuclear reaction rates might be wrong, but laboratory measurements have closed most loopholes. Or there might be new physics, such as decaying particles in the early universe. The problem has persisted for over forty years.

The second is the S eight tension, a cousin of the Hubble tension. S eight is a measure of how clumpy matter is today. The microwave background, with the standard model, predicts a certain clumpiness. Some measurements of the present universe, using the subtle distortion of galaxy shapes by gravitational lensing, found slightly less clumpiness, by about two or three standard deviations. In recent years, newer analyses, particularly from the Kilo-Degree Survey in 2025, have reduced the discrepancy, and many now regard it as largely resolved, though not everyone agrees.

The third concerns the microwave background itself. On the very largest scales, its pattern shows a few oddities. There is a large cold spot in the southern sky, colder and larger than expected. There is an apparent alignment of the largest patterns with each other and with the plane of the solar system, nicknamed the axis of evil. There is an asymmetry between the two halves of the sky, and a lack of correlation on the very largest angles. Each anomaly has a probability of perhaps one in a hundred or one in a thousand in the standard model. But with so many possible features to look at, some unusual ones are bound to appear by chance, a problem statisticians call the look-elsewhere effect. Proposed explanations range from chance, to foreground contamination, to exotic ideas like a supervoid along the line of sight to the cold spot, or traces of a pre-inflationary universe. The Planck satellite confirmed the anomalies exist in its data but could not determine whether they are significant.

The fourth is the EDGES signal. In 2018, the EDGES team reported a dip in the radio spectrum at about seventy-eight megahertz, interpreted as absorption by hydrogen gas at the time of the first stars, about a hundred and eighty million years after the beginning. The timing was plausible, but the dip was more than twice as deep as allowed by standard physics, implying either colder gas or a brighter radio background than expected. Proposals included interactions between dark matter and ordinary matter that cooled the gas. Critics questioned whether the signal could be an artefact of the instrument or of the way the overwhelming galactic radio emission was subtracted. In 2022, the SARAS three experiment, floating on lakes in southern India, reported no evidence for the signal, disfavouring it at high confidence. Other experiments, such as REACH in South Africa, are now taking data.

Others include the missing baryon problem, in which, for many years, astronomers could find only about half of the ordinary matter that the early universe says should exist in the present universe; observations of fast radio bursts in 2020 and later located most of it in thin, hot gas between galaxies, largely resolving it. There are several small-scale problems of dark matter: simulations of cold dark matter predict galaxies with dense, cuspy centres and many small satellites, while real galaxies often show flatter cores and fewer satellites. Many astronomers now think these are explained by the effects of stars and exploding supernovae on gas, plus the difficulty of seeing very faint galaxies, but some see them as hints that dark matter has properties beyond the simplest model. And there is the mild excess of very massive galaxy clusters and some mass estimates of early galaxies from Webb.
Each of these puzzles may dissolve with better data. But each is also a place where something new could be hiding, and cosmologists watch them closely.
